description: Current and former leaders of ITACUBE, the nanosatellite initiative of the Instituto Tecnológico de Aeronáutica (ITA), Brazil. We design, build and operate small satellites, and bring skills in SAR and optical remote sensing, geospatial data, hydrology, predictive modelling, web development, UX design and science communication. With IARA, we turn NISAR radar data into maps and stories about mining, floods and drought in the Amazon, for the communities and agencies that face them.
summary:
Few places hold as much life, or face as much pressure, as the Amazon. In the words of the American writer Henry David Thoreau, “In wildness is the preservation of the world.”

IARA is a web app that turns radar satellite data into maps and stories about three threats to the Amazon: illegal gold mining in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory, floods on the Rio Negro in Manaus, and drought in the lakes of Manaquiri. We built mosaics from NISAR L-band and S-band scenes and added Sentinel-1 and ALOS-2 archives, so users can compare an area before and after an event. L-band passes through the canopy, so cleared mining ground shows a sharp drop in backscatter, and open water appears dark even under heavy cloud. The map also shows river levels, GloFAS and GEOGLOWS flood forecasts and the locations of potential illegal mining sites. An assistant answers questions and moves the map for you. Clouds and smoke hide the Amazon from optical satellites for much of the year, but radar keeps recording, and IARA gives that record to the people who live with these risks and the agencies that respond to them.

Overview

Figure 1. Hero shot of IARA. Full screen of the app with the NISAR mosaic on the map, with the IARA assistant bar at the bottom.

For much of the year the Amazon sits under cloud and smoke, and optical satellites lose sight of the ground just when people need them most. Radar keeps seeing it. IARA is a web app that turns NASA/ISRO NISAR radar data into maps and stories anyone can read, focused on three threats: illegal gold mining in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory, Rio Negro floods in Manaus, and drought in the lakes of Manaquiri.

Users open a case, read what is happening to the people there, and compare radar images of the same place before and after an event. Live deforestation alerts from INPE DETER and Global Forest Watch RADD, the Rio Negro gauge record since 1902 and river flood forecasts sit on the same map. You can ask the IARA assistant a question in Portuguese or English, and it answers and moves the map to show you.

What IARA delivers:
  • NISAR L-band and S-band mosaics of the three areas, built from 265 scenes acquired between June and November 2026;
  • Before and after radar comparisons from Sentinel-1, NISAR and ALOS archives;
  • Seven-day flood chance for any river point, computed live from GEOGLOWS ensemble forecasts and
  • An AI assistant that controls the map and answers only from sourced case data.

Figure 2. The three case cards side by side: Yanomami mining, Manaus flood, Manaquiri drought.

How radar reads the Amazon

Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sends its own microwave pulse and records the echo, day or night, through cloud. What comes back depends on the surface:

  • Forest scatters the pulse in many directions and part of it returns, so forest looks bright;
  • Bare soil and mining pits send little back, so a new clearing shows up as a dark patch;
  • Calm water reflects the pulse away like a mirror, so rivers and lakes look black.

That single rule drives all three cases. In the Yanomami land, dark patches spread into the bright forest. In Manaus, the black of the river grows over the city during a flood. In Manaquiri, the black of the lakes shrinks into the grey of a dry lake bed.

Figure 3. Diagram of what the radar sees over forest, cleared soil, flooded forest and open water.

Frequency bands

Longer wavelengths go deeper into vegetation. Shorter ones respond to the top of the canopy and to the water surface. NISAR is the first mission to carry both an L-band and an S-band radar, so IARA can show the same scene at two wavelengths.

Figure 4. Radar frequency bands description.

Polarization adds a second layer. HH and VV respond to surfaces like water and bare soil. HV responds to volume scattering inside vegetation, which helps separate forest from cleared land. The NISAR L-band mosaics use HH and HV together.

The three cases

  1. Gold mining in the Yanomami territory: Brazil's largest Indigenous land, 96,650 km² with 27,228 residents, has been hit by industrial-scale illegal mining since 2018. The destroyed area grew 309% between October 2018 and December 2022, from 1,236 to 5,053 hectares (Hutukara Associação Yanomami). In IARA you can follow the series year by year, compare each year with a 2016 radar baseline, see DETER alerts as they come in, and fly to the main mining corridors.
  2. Floods in Manaus: the Rio Negro at Manaus reached 30.02 m on June 16, 2021, its highest level in 119 years. Thousands of families live in stilt houses along the city's streams, where the water arrives first. Four of the five largest floods on record happened in 2009 or later. IARA shows the gauge record since 1902 against the official alert and flood levels, radar pairs of each flood, and live GloFAS and GEOGLOWS forecasts.
  3. Droughts in Manaquiri: about 60 km from Manaus, communities like Andiroba, Jutaí and Janauacá reach town by boat across a network of lakes. In 2023 and 2024 those lakes turned to mud, fish died and some communities lost their water supply. On October 9, 2024 the Rio Negro fell to 12.11 m, the lowest in 122 years. IARA shows the open water shrinking on radar and ranks the communities by distance to town and dependence on a lake.

How we built it


How IARA Works

IARA starts from open satellite radar, deforestation alerts and river data. Scripts turn the radar scenes into mosaics, before-and-after pairs and seven-day flood chances. A web app brings them together in a live map, three case stories and an AI assistant, and a single link shares any view with communities, agencies and the press.

Radar mosaics

Our scripts query the ASF Search API for NISAR Level 2 GCOV scenes over each area and download their georeferenced browse images. They keep dual-polarization scenes, remove the dark fringes at swath edges, balance colors between scenes so no seams show, and stack them from oldest to newest. The current mosaics use 199 scenes for the Yanomami land, 31 for Manaus and 35 for Manaquiri. Sentinel-1 and ALOS mosaics follow the same approach.

Before and after

For each year in a case's series, the app requests Sentinel-1 terrain-corrected images from the Microsoft Planetary Computer, cropped to exactly the same box, and shows them with a slider. When no radar pair exists for a date, it falls back to a MODIS image from NASA Worldview and says so.

Live layers and forecasts

DETER alerts come live from INPE TerraBrasilis and RADD forest-disturbance alerts from Global Forest Watch, along with GloFAS flood probability and NASA GIBS MODIS/VIIRS flood maps. River forecasts come from GEOGLOWS for seven reference points and for any point the user clicks.

The IARA assistant

The assistant sends the question and the state of the map to a language model through a small Cloudflare Worker. The model can call tools to open a case, switch tabs, move the camera or turn on a layer, and the browser runs them. It is told to answer facts only from the case data and to say when it does not know. Without the Worker, it falls back to offline keyword rules.

Built with React, TypeScript and MapLibre, running as a static site.

Predictive models

IARA also looks ahead. We trained three predictive models, one for each case, and exported their results as lightweight JSON files that the web app reads. All three use a strict temporal holdout, so nothing from the future leaks into training, and the metrics were declared before training.

(I) Mining risk in the Yanomami territory (XGBoost)

  1. Target: the probability that a pixel loses forest in the next year, used as a proxy for the expansion of mining. The label comes from Hansen Global Forest Change v1.12 (Landsat). According to the Hutukara Yanomami Association, mining accounts for more than 90% of the forest loss in the territory.
  2. Features: eleven per pixel: SRTM elevation and slope, Sentinel-1 RTC backscatter statistics in VV and VH, the cumulative Hansen loss in a 1 km buffer up to year t, the distance to the nearest earlier loss pixel, the CHIRPS rainfall of the year, and the normalized year.
  3. Model: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost on GPU, histogram method). The prediction is the sigmoid of the sum of the tree outputs, and training minimizes the binary logistic loss with quadratic regularization. Positive pixels are rare, so the positive class is weighted by n⁻/n⁺. Training stops early after 50 rounds without improvement in PR-AUC.
  4. Quality: on the temporal holdout the model reaches a ROC-AUC of 0.797 and a PR-AUC of 0.157, with a Brier score of 0.080. Among the 5% of pixels with the highest predicted risk we capture 51.8% of all the pixels that actually lost forest.Two features carry almost all the gain: the cumulative loss in the buffer (0.48) and the distance to earlier loss (0.42). Mining advances from fronts that are already open.

 (II) Rio Negro level at Manaus (SARIMAX and LSTM)

  1. Target: the daily level of the Rio Negro at the Porto de Manaus gauge (ANA station 14990000), at horizons of 7, 30 and 365 days. The record runs from 1902 to 2014, and 2010 to 2014 is the holdout (1,825 days).
  2. Exogenous inputs:  three yearly Fourier terms (m = 365.25) and two ENSO indices, the Niño 3.4 z-score and the SOI, both lagged by 180 days.
  3. Baseline: SARIMAX. Order (p, d, q) = (1, 1, 0) with no seasonal part, because the Fourier terms absorb the seasonality. It is fitted with L-BFGS and gives the forecast with its 80% confidence band (P10 to P90).
  4. Challenger: LSTM. A window of the past 365 days, joined with the exogenous inputs, predicts the level h days ahead. The network has 2 layers with hidden size 128, dropout 0.1 and a linear head. It is trained with AdamW (learning rate 10⁻³), Huber loss, 30 epochs and batch size 512. The z-score normalization is fitted on the training split only.
  5. Quality: the LSTM at 7 days is the best model: RMSE 0.200 m and a Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) of 0.998. At 30 days the RMSE is 0.958 m with NSE 0.949. An NSE of 1 would be a perfect prediction, and above 0.7 is considered good in operational hydrology; every model stays above that line. The peak RMSE is the RMSE on the days above the 90th percentile of the observed level. It measures the error at the flood peak, which is where the human decision matters, and for the LSTM it is 0.117 m at 7 days and 0.304 m at 30 days.The 365-day SARIMAX forecast is read against the official SGB levels for Manaus: 27.50 m for alert, 29.00 m for flood and 29.97 m for severe flood.

(III) Isolation of communities in Manaquiri (logistic regression and Monte Carlo)

  1. Target: the daily probability that a riverside community (Andiroba, Jutaí, Barro Alto or Janauacá) is isolated, given the river level.
  2. Persistent label: a single day below the threshold τ of a community does not mean isolation. A day is labelled isolated only after seven consecutive days below τ. The threshold is the historical quantile calibrated for each community: 19.86 m for Andiroba, 18.36 m for Jutaí, 17.38 m for Barro Alto and 16.36 m for Janauacá.
  3. Logistic classifier: the inputs are the distance between the level and the threshold and the month of the year as sine and cosine. It uses C = 1 and balanced class weights, with an 80/20 temporal split.
  4. Monte Carlo over the level forecast: the P10, P50, P90 band of the level forecast is treated as a Gaussian on each day, with μ = p50 and σ = (p90 − p10) / (2 Φ⁻¹(0.9)). We simulate 2,000 trajectories, apply the classifier to each one and add up the isolated days in the 365-day horizon. The result is reported as P10, P50, P90 and mean.
  5. Quality and forecast: the ROC-AUC is close to 1 for the four communities. That reflects the fact that the persistent label is almost deterministic given the observed level. The value of the model is in the Monte Carlo step, which carries the uncertainty of the level forecast and turns a probability per day into a distribution of isolated days: from a median of 42 days for Andiroba (36 to 49) to 10 days for Janauacá (6 to 14).

(IV) Settings and limitations

  • The legacy ANA service stops returning data after December 30, 2014. The level model uses 112 years of observations (1902 to 2014), which cover the full seasonality and several ENSO cycles, but 2015 to 2026 does not enter as observed training data.
  • RADD alerts, derived from Sentinel-1, would be the ideal target for the mining model, but their bulk download needs authentication that did not fit the hackathon window. We used Hansen GFC instead, which is yearly but dense.
  • Monthly CHIRPS rainfall was planned as an exogenous input for the river level. The model uses ENSO (Niño 3.4 and SOI) as the climate proxy for the Rio Negro basin.
